You know, Hawaii's issue when we talk to the state health director, Dr. Libby Chars, is that they could do 80,000 vaccines a week, but right now they're limited to far less than that because of just the doses that they're getting on the federal side. You know, I think this is a really important point. We were not sure whether the sort of limiting factor was going to be our logistical capacity in the state of Hawaii or was it going to be the supply of vaccines. And I think if Johnson & Johnson gets its emergency use authorization, as we expect, that they will. That's just a one-jab thing which makes for way easier logistics. I visited the the Queens facility and the Pier 2 facility and both of them are telling me that the Johnson and Johnson vaccine will be a game changer and hundreds of millions of doses will be available. So I'm somewhat hopeful about the availability of vaccine over the next six weeks. turn_text: You know, one of the other areas of course that has been impacted by this has been just schools and the ability for our children to be in schools. We know that you have said vocally that you believe that we should be getting students back into the classroom. We're looking at some of these numbers that we're seeing in our daily COVID cases. Obviously the numbers are going down. What are your thoughts and have you had any discussions with education leaders to see how we can get students back into the classroom?

Yeah, you know, this was an interesting process over the last couple of weeks. I've been talking to the governor, the superintendent, through staff, talked with Dr. Char, legislative leaders, mayors, and others. And everybody seems to be in agreement, you know, we ought to open the schools as soon as possible. You know, the CDC changed their guidelines to basically say six feet of social distancing is not a prerequisite. It should be done to the greatest extent practical. And that is a big change in policy. And what that means is in places where there's low COVID, It is okay and universal masking. It is okay to have kids three feet apart, as long as they're masked and you're in a place where there's very, very low COVID. I had a constructive conversation with Corey Rosenley from HSTA. I've been talking to both UPW and HGA. And I think the good news is that everybody is saying that they want to reopen in-person schools as quickly as possible. Now come the logistics. And this is where I worry a bit is that if we have a collective determination to reopen the schools, you know, that takes some doing. It takes curriculum changes. It takes the reconfiguration of physical space. it takes covid protocols new training for teachers and principals and and other school staff so if we've decided to do this and i think we have collectively although that's not a formal decision but i haven't talked to a major education or government leader who doesn't agree we should re-open the schools as soon as it's possible, then the logistics are going to be tremendously challenging. And if we don't get started right away, then we're going to lose the fourth quarter of the academic year. And so the kind of logical pivot point would be for us to kind of operationalize some of this stuff so that we could have spring break and then try to do in-person learning to the greatest extent possible. Now, I just got to say this. There are certain teachers who are going to be needing reasonable accommodations because of their health issues, and that's a real thing. And there are parents who may want to continue with online for their kids, and that's a real thing. And so I'm not suggesting that we should flip a switch and just reopen the schools. I am suggesting that if the COVID rates stay this low or even continue on their downward trajectory, we have to be ready for the possibility that we could actually save the fourth quarter of this academic year. It'll take a lot of doing, and it'll take a lot of negotiating, and one of the conversations I had with Corey Rosinley was, look, we should do this all within the context of collective bargaining. But I think we can do this if we have our shared values, which is we're going to respect our teachers. We're going to keep all of our school staff safe. We're going to keep the COVID rates low. But, and these kids need to be doing in-person learning because, you know, as parents, I think there's a broad recognition that online learning is not as good as in-person learning.
